analogy.p: Imagine a satnav that, whenever you pass a junction, recalculates the route and tells you the next turn. You follow it, it recalculates, and each time you are a bit closer to the destination until you arrive. Iteration is the same: each answer is fed back into the formula to give a better guess, and the guesses settle on the root just as the car settles on the address. A formula that converges is like a satnav that works; a formula that diverges is like one that keeps sending you further away. The analogy breaks down because a satnav knows the destination in advance, whereas in iteration you do not know the root until the sequence settles, and a car stops when it arrives but the iteration only ever gets closer without ever stopping by itself.
analogy.t: Homing in with a satnav that keeps re-routing

bullets: An **equation** is solved when you find x so that both sides are equal; a **root** of f(x) = 0 is a value of x where f(x) = 0, i.e. where the graph crosses the x-axis.
Iteration is used when an algebraic method does not work, typically for cubic equations and equations mixing powers of x with x itself.
An **iterative formula** gives the next value in terms of the previous one, for example x(n+1) = (3 - x(n)^3) / 5.
You choose a **starting value** x0 (or x1), calculate the next value, and keep going; the sequence of values is a **sequence defined by a recurrence relation**.
If the method works the values **converge**: they settle towards one number, which is the root, accurate to as many digits as you continue.
The answer is **approximate**, so questions always say 'to 2 decimal places' or 'to 3 significant figures' or ask for a stated number of iterations.
Computers use exactly the same idea, which is why this is called a **numerical method**.
core.h: What iteration is and why we need it
core.p: **Iteration** means repeating the same calculation over and over, feeding each answer back in as the next input, so that the answers get closer and closer to the solution of an equation. Many equations, such as x^3 + 5x - 3 = 0, cannot be solved by factorising, by the quadratic formula or by rearranging to make x the subject, because x appears in more than one form (x^3 and x). Iteration gets around this by turning the equation into an **iterative formula** and using a calculator to home in on a **root** (a value of x that makes the equation true). The answer is always an **approximation**, but you can make it as accurate as you like by doing more steps. The Edexcel specification asks you to find approximate solutions to equations numerically using iteration, and on a Higher paper this normally comes as a short chain of linked marks.

bullets: x(n) is read 'x subscript n'; the small n is **not** multiplied, it is a position label.
If x0 = 1 then **x1 = g(x0)**, **x2 = g(x1)**, **x3 = g(x2)** and so on, where g is the right-hand side of the formula.
The same formula is used every time; only the input changes.
If a question says 'find x2' starting from x0, you must do **two** applications of the formula, not one.
Always copy the formula exactly as given into your working, substituting the previous value in brackets, e.g. (3 - (0.6)^3) / 5.
Keep **full calculator values** for each x(n) while working; only round at the very end, because rounding early can change later digits.
Present results as a neat list: x1 = 0.6, x2 = 0.5568, x3 = 0.565475...
core.h: Notation: x(n), x(n+1) and the starting value
core.p: The letter **n** is just a counter. x(n) means 'the n-th value in the list' and x(n+1) means 'the next value after it'. So the formula x(n+1) = (3 - x(n)^3) / 5 says: take any value, cube it, subtract the result from 3, divide by 5, and that gives the next value. You are usually told the starting value, written x0 = 0 or x1 = 0. Be careful with the subscripts: if the question says x0 = 0 then x1 is the first answer you calculate, but if it says x1 = 0 then x2 is the first answer you calculate. Writing a table of n against x(n) keeps this straight and earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips later.

bullets: Step 1: type the starting value, e.g. **0**, then press **=**.
Step 2: type the formula using **ANS**, e.g. **(3 - ANS^3) / 5**, then press **=**: the display is x1 = 0.6.
Step 3: press **=** again: the display is x2 = 0.5568; again: x3 = 0.565475...; again: x4 = 0.563836...
Use **brackets** around the whole numerator, otherwise the calculator divides only the last term by 5.
Write down each value to **at least 4 or 5 decimal places** (more than the accuracy asked for) so the examiner can see the sequence settling.
Check x1 by hand once to make sure the calculator formula was typed correctly.
If the question wants a table of values, show n, x(n) in two columns; the table itself is evidence for the method mark.
core.h: Using the calculator ANS key step by step
core.p: The quickest and most reliable way to iterate is the **ANS key**, which stores the last answer. Type the starting value and press equals so ANS holds it. Then type the formula using ANS wherever x(n) appears, and press equals; the display shows x1 and now ANS holds x1. Pressing equals again repeats the whole formula with the new ANS, giving x2, then x3, and so on. You never retype numbers, which removes copying errors, and you can write down each value in turn. For the formula x(n+1) = (3 - x(n)^3) / 5 with x0 = 0, you type 0 =, then (3 - ANS^3) / 5 =, then press = again repeatedly. The calculator automatically uses full accuracy internally.

bullets: Aim to get **x = something** with x on its own on the left; the 'something' may still contain x.
Do the same operation to **both sides** at each step and show every step; marks are for method, not just the final line.
Example: x^3 - x - 1 = 0 gives x^3 = x + 1, so **x = cube root of (x + 1)**, which becomes x(n+1) = cube root of (x(n) + 1).
Example: x^2 - 3x - 1 = 0 gives x^2 = 3x + 1; divide by x: **x = 3 + 1/x**, so x(n+1) = 3 + 1 / x(n).
Check you have not divided by x incorrectly: x^2 - 3x - 1 = 0 divided by x gives x - 3 - 1/x = 0, so x = 3 + 1/x. This is correct.
For 'show that' questions the final line must **match the given formula exactly**, so finish by writing x(n+1) = ... with the subscripts.
Different rearrangements of the same equation have the **same root** but different rates of convergence (some diverge).
core.h: Rearranging an equation into an iterative formula
core.p: A common Higher question gives an equation and asks you to **show that** it can be rearranged into a given iterative formula. You must start from the equation and make small, clearly justified algebraic steps until you reach exactly the printed formula, with the equation sign balanced at every stage. To rearrange, isolate one occurrence of x, so the equation becomes x = g(x). For example, from x^3 + 5x - 3 = 0, move the cube term and the number: 5x = 3 - x^3, then divide by 5: x = (3 - x^3) / 5. Then replace the right-hand x by x(n) and the left-hand x by x(n+1), because the output of one step is the input of the next. The same equation can be rearranged in several ways, and not every rearrangement converges, which is why the question always tells you which formula to use.

bullets: First rewrite the equation as **f(x) = 0** with everything on one side, e.g. x^3 + 5x - 3 = 0.
Evaluate f at both end points and write the values clearly, e.g. **f(0) = -3, f(1) = 3**.
State the conclusion: 'there is a **change of sign**, and f(x) is **continuous**, so there is a root between 0 and 1'.
Both values must be correct: a wrong sign at one end loses the mark, so check each with care (a negative number cubed stays negative).
The interval is a statement about **at least one** root; there could be more than one in the interval, but a change of sign guarantees at least one.
Use the same method with a very narrow interval to prove a root to a given accuracy (see the rounding section).
If the signs are the **same** at both ends, you cannot conclude anything: there may be no root or an even number of roots.
core.h: Showing a root lies in an interval: change of sign
core.p: Before iterating, you are often asked to **show that the equation f(x) = 0 has a root between a and b**. The method is to substitute the two end values into f(x) and show that one answer is negative and the other is positive. A **change of sign** means the graph of y = f(x) is below the x-axis at one end and above it at the other. Because the graph of a continuous function has no gaps or jumps, it must cross the x-axis somewhere in between, and the crossing point is the root. For f(x) = x^3 + 5x - 3: f(0) = -3 and f(1) = 1 + 5 - 3 = 3, a change of sign, so there is a root between 0 and 1. A full-mark answer states the two values, says there is a change of sign, and states that f is continuous (the graph is a smooth curve) so a root lies in the interval.

bullets: **Continuous** means the graph can be drawn without lifting the pen: all polynomials such as quadratics and cubics are continuous.
A change of sign between a and b on a continuous graph **proves** at least one root in the interval.
y = 1/x is **not continuous** at x = 0: f(-1) = -1 and f(1) = 1 change sign, yet there is no solution of 1/x = 0.
A repeated root (the curve just touches the axis, as for (x - 2)^2 = 0 at x = 2) does **not** produce a sign change, so the test cannot detect it.
Two roots in the same interval cancel the change of sign: f could go negative to positive to negative, ending with the same sign as it began.
Choose end points close together to be sure there is only one root in that interval.
Link: a root of f(x) = 0 is where the **graph of y = f(x) crosses the x-axis**, so this is a graph idea in disguise.
core.h: Why a change of sign works, and when it can fail
core.p: The idea behind a change of sign is that a **continuous function** takes every value between f(a) and f(b); if f(a) is negative and f(b) is positive then 0 must be taken somewhere between a and b. On the graph, you cannot get from below the axis to above it without crossing it. The test can fail in two situations. If the graph is not continuous, for example y = 1/x which jumps from very negative to very positive at x = 0, there is a change of sign between -1 and 1 but no root. And if the curve touches the axis without crossing (a repeated root, such as x^2 = 0 at x = 0), there is no sign change even though there is a root. For GCSE questions the functions are smooth polynomials, so the test is reliable, but quoting that the function is continuous earns the reasoning mark.

bullets: To 1 decimal place, the interval is the value +/- 0.05; to 2 decimal places, +/- 0.005; to 3 decimal places, +/- 0.0005.
Example: root = 1.3 to 1 d.p. means the true root is between **1.25 and 1.35**.
Calculate f at both **boundaries**, state the signs, and conclude the root lies in the interval, hence rounds to the stated value.
Do not just show that the iterations agree to 2 d.p.; that is evidence but is not a proof, because iterated values can agree and still be on one side of a rounding boundary.
Decide which interval end is which: the lower boundary is the value minus the half unit, the upper boundary is plus.
Values very close to the root give a tiny f value, so use full calculator accuracy to get the sign right.
State the final answer clearly with the units of accuracy: 'x = 0.56 (2 d.p.)'.
core.h: Giving the root to a stated accuracy and proving it
core.p: Once the iteration values settle, you give the root rounded to the accuracy asked. A quick check is that successive values agree to that many decimal places, but to **prove** the rounding is right you must use a change of sign on the boundaries of the rounding interval. To show a root is 0.56 correct to 2 decimal places, every number that rounds to 0.56 lies in the interval 0.555 to 0.565, so show f(0.555) and f(0.565) have opposite signs. Here f(0.555) = -0.054 (negative) and f(0.565) = 0.005 (positive), so the root lies between 0.555 and 0.565 and rounds to 0.56 to 2 decimal places. This boundary test is a favourite 2-mark Higher question. For significant figures the same idea applies, using the interval half a unit either side of the last digit.

bullets: **Converge**: successive values differ by less and less and agree to more and more decimal places.
**Diverge**: successive values get further apart or grow without limit, so the method fails.
Convergence can be **one-sided** (values rise steadily towards the root) or **oscillating** (alternately above and below the root).
Rearrangements that fail to converge are not wrong algebra; they simply do not home in on the root, so you should use the one provided.
A good test in the exam: compare two successive values to the accuracy needed; if they agree, stop.
The speed matters: the formula that converges fastest needs fewer steps to reach the required accuracy.
core.p: An iteration **converges** if the values get closer and closer to a single number as n increases; that number is the root. It **diverges** if the values move away from any single value, growing larger and larger (or swinging with increasing size) so no root is found. Whether a rearrangement converges depends on the formula. For x(n+1) = (3 - x(n)^3) / 5 starting at 0 the values are 0.6, 0.5568, 0.5655, 0.5638, 0.5641, 0.5641: they oscillate above and below the root with decreasing swings and settle at 0.5641. For the rearrangement x(n+1) = x(n)^3 - 1 starting at 1, the values are 0, -1, -2, -9, -730: they diverge. You do not need to prove convergence at GCSE; you observe the pattern from the table and, if asked, say what happens.

bullets: Method: find an interval with a **sign change**, test a value inside, **keep the sub-interval that still has the sign change**, repeat.
Each stage improves the accuracy by one decimal place if you test tenths, then hundredths, and so on.
Record x, f(x) and the sign in a table; the marks are for correct values and correct decisions.
To decide the rounding to 2 d.p., always test the **half-way** value (such as 0.565) rather than only 0.56 and 0.57.
Decimal search needs no rearranging, but it takes more evaluations than iteration with the ANS key.
Both methods give an **approximate** solution; the exam will say which one to use.
core.h: Decimal search (trial and improvement) as a related method
core.p: Trial and improvement, also called decimal search, finds a root by testing values and narrowing an interval using the sign of f(x). Start with an integer interval where f changes sign, then test the midpoint or the next tenth, keep the half where the sign still changes, and repeat with hundredths and then thousandths. This is a numerical method, like iteration, but it uses the change of sign directly rather than a formula. For f(x) = x^3 + 5x - 3: f(0.5) = -0.375 and f(0.6) = 0.216, so the root is between 0.5 and 0.6; f(0.56) = -0.0244 and f(0.57) = 0.0352, so the root is between 0.56 and 0.57; this shows the root is 0.56 to 2 d.p. only after also checking f(0.565) = 0.005 (positive), which puts the root below 0.565. Show a table of x and f(x) with the sign each time.

bullets: (a) Change of sign: write f(a), f(b), the signs, and a concluding sentence.
(b) Rearrangement: start from the original equation, show each step, finish on the given formula.
(c) Iterations: show x1, x2, x3 with substituted values and answers to at least 4 d.p.
(d) Final answer: round to the stated accuracy, and if asked 'show that' use a boundary check.
A '**3 iterations**' question means apply the formula three times from the starting value, ending at x3.
If the question says 'x1 = 1', the first value you calculate is x2; always check which subscript is given.
Write units of accuracy such as '(2 decimal places)' after the final answer.
If marks are allocated for a table, give a column for n and a column for x(n).
core.h: A complete 'show that' and 'use iteration' routine
core.p: Higher questions on iteration are usually in three or four parts, and the same routine works every time. Part (a): show a root lies in an interval, using a change of sign. Part (b): show the equation can be rearranged to the given iterative formula. Part (c): use the formula with a given starting value to find x1, x2, x3 (a table). Part (d): give the root to a stated accuracy, sometimes with a boundary change-of-sign proof. Read the question carefully for how many iterations are wanted and the accuracy needed. A table of working should be printed on your paper; the examiner rewards clear lines such as x1 = (3 - 0^3)/5 = 0.6. It is crucial to avoid rounding in the middle of the iteration, and to write the final answer to the accuracy asked, even if the calculator shows more digits.

bullets: A start inside the **interval with a sign change** is sensible because it is near the root.
For a convergent formula the final answer does not depend on which starting value you use (within reason).
A start of 0 is easy to type but can cause division by zero if the formula has 1/x in it (x(n+1) = 3 + 1/x(n) starting at 0 is impossible).
The starting value is x0 in some papers and x1 in others; always follow the subscripts in the question.
If your values go negative where the formula needs a square root or cube root, check the sign of the starting value.
For comparison, x(n+1) = 3 + 1/x(n) with x0 = 3 gives 3.3333, 3.3, 3.3030, 3.3028, 3.3028: converging to 3.3028.
A table of values from a different starting value showing the same limit is good evidence of reliability.
core.h: Choosing and testing a starting value
core.p: The starting value is normally given, but if you must choose one, use a value inside the interval where you showed the root lies, or the end point at which the function is closest to zero. For an interval from 0 to 1 either end or the middle (0.5) is a sensible start. A starting value close to the root usually converges faster, but for a convergent formula even a poor start still converges, only taking a few more steps. If the iteration diverges from a sensible start, the formula is not suitable, and you try a different rearrangement. In an exam you are normally told 'use x0 = 1' so you do not need to choose.

bullets: The equation f(x) = 0 has roots where y = f(x) **crosses the x-axis**.
The rearranged equation x = g(x) has solutions where **y = x meets y = g(x)**; the same x-value is the root.
A gentle slope of g near the root (gradient between -1 and 1) tends to give convergence; a steep slope gives divergence.
A negative gradient gives an oscillating, cobweb-type sequence, as in x(n+1) = (3 - x(n)^3)/5.
A positive gradient gives a one-sided staircase, as in x(n+1) = cube root of (x(n) + 1).
You do not need to draw these at GCSE, but you may be asked to **explain** why the sequence is moving towards a particular value.
Graphical solutions of equations, sequences and function notation all connect to this topic.
core.h: Interpreting iteration graphically (the link to graphs)
core.p: The root of x = g(x) is where the line y = x meets the curve y = g(x), so iteration can be seen as a sequence of steps between the two graphs. Starting from x0, go up to the curve to read g(x0), across to the line y = x to turn that output into the next input x1, and repeat. Whether the steps spiral inward (converge) or outward (diverge) depends on the gradient of the curve at the intersection: shallow curves give convergence. At GCSE you are not asked to draw these staircase and cobweb diagrams, but understanding them explains why some rearrangements work and others do not. It also links iteration to the work on solving equations graphically, where the solution of f(x) = 0 is where y = f(x) meets the x-axis.

bullets: Sequences: **x(n+1) = g(x(n))** is a term-to-term rule, so the language of 'terms' and 'sequences' applies.
Accuracy: be fluent with rounding to decimal places and to significant figures.
Algebra: rearranging to make x the subject is a core Higher skill that is tested inside iteration.
Graphs: the roots of f(x) = 0 are the x-intercepts, and the iteration can be checked against a sketch.
Real-life contexts: lengths of a box or a tank satisfying a cubic equation, where the answer needs units.
Higher tier paper structure: iteration questions usually appear on Paper 2 or 3 (calculator papers) because they need a calculator; Paper 1 has no calculator.
Always read whether the question asks for the **solution to the equation** or just the **value of x(n)**.
core.h: Link to other topics and exam variations
core.p: Iteration links to sequences (an iterative formula is a **term-to-term rule**), to graphs of cubic and quadratic functions (roots as x-intercepts), to rearranging formulae (making x the subject), to accuracy and rounding (decimal places and significant figures), and to proof. Typical variations include: a quadratic such as x^2 - 3x - 1 = 0 rearranged to x = 3 + 1/x, whose positive root is 3.3028 to 4 d.p.; a cubic with a root in a stated interval; and a 'real-life' context where a length or time satisfies a cubic equation. Sometimes the question will ask you to explain why a particular value of x is the solution, e.g. because successive iterations are equal to the required accuracy. Always give your answer in the form the question requests.

exam: **Command words:** 'Show that' means prove using method and end on the given result; 'Use iteration' means apply the formula with the ANS key; 'Find' means calculate; 'Explain' needs a reason.

**Typical marks:** change of sign 2 marks (both values correct, with conclusion); rearrangement 2 to 3 marks (one per correct step); iteration values 2 to 3 marks; final accuracy 1 to 2 marks. Total often 5 to 7 marks.
**1 mark:** one correct function value or one correct x(n); **2 marks:** two correct function values with a stated change of sign, or a correct x1 and x2.
**Model phrase:** 'f(0) = -3 and f(1) = 3. There is a change of sign and f(x) is continuous, so there is a root between 0 and 1.'
**Model phrase for accuracy:** 'f(0.555) = -0.054 and f(0.565) = 0.005. There is a change of sign, so the root lies between 0.555 and 0.565 and is 0.56 correct to 2 decimal places.'
Show **substituted values** in your working: x2 = (3 - 0.6^3) / 5 = 0.5568, rather than writing only the answer.
Do not round in the middle; keep full calculator values and quote your table to at least 4 decimal places.
Read the **subscript** carefully: x0, x1, x2 mean different things; a 'find x3' question needs three applications of the formula from x0.
On calculator papers the ANS key is the intended method; on a non-calculator paper iteration is not examined with hard arithmetic.
Check the final answer is **in the interval** you showed earlier, as a quick sense check.
Revision tip: practise the same two equations (x^3 + 5x - 3 = 0 and x^3 - x - 1 = 0) until the routine is automatic.

mistakes.r: Keep the full calculator value in ANS, and round only the final answer to the accuracy requested.
mistakes.w: Rounding each x(n) to 2 decimal places during the iteration, so the later values drift.

mistakes.r: Calculate both end values (f(0) = -3 and f(1) = 3), state there is a change of sign, and conclude there is a root between 0 and 1.
mistakes.w: Showing a root lies between 0 and 1 by writing only f(0) = -3.

mistakes.r: Use brackets around the numerator: (3 - ANS^3) / 5, otherwise only the last term is divided by 5.
mistakes.w: Typing (3 - ANS^3 / 5 into the calculator without brackets.

mistakes.r: Prove it with a boundary change of sign: f(0.555) < 0 and f(0.565) > 0, so the root is in that interval and rounds to 0.56.
mistakes.w: Claiming 'the root is 0.56 because x4 and x5 are both 0.56'.

mistakes.r: If the starting value is x1 the first value to calculate is x2; if it is x0, the first is x1.
mistakes.w: Mixing up subscripts: given x1 = 1, working out x1 again as the first answer.

mistakes.r: Rearrange carefully: x^2 = 3x + 1, so x = 3 + 1/x (dividing every term by x).
Keep going until the last line is exactly x(n+1) = the given expression, with correct subscripts.
mistakes.w: Stopping the 'show that' rearrangement before reaching the given formula.

mistakes.r: Write 'change of sign, f is continuous, so a root lies between ...'.
mistakes.w: Using the change of sign test without mentioning continuity or concluding.

mistakes.r: Round to the accuracy asked in the question, e.g. 0.56 to 2 decimal places.
mistakes.w: Giving the answer to far too many decimal places ('0.5640993...').

summary: Edexcel Higher asks you to find approximate solutions to equations numerically using iteration: show a root lies in an interval by a change of sign, rearrange an equation into the form x(n+1) = g(x(n)), use your calculator (ANS key) to repeat the formula, and give the root to a stated accuracy with a justification. It matters because it is the only method for solving equations like x^3 + 5x - 3 = 0 that cannot be factorised or rearranged, and it appears as a multi-mark 'show that' and 'use iteration' question on Higher papers.

terms.d: Repeating a calculation, using each output as the next input, to find an approximate solution of an equation.
A formula of the form x(n+1) = g(x(n)) that gives each term from the previous term.
A value of x for which f(x) = 0; the x-coordinate where the graph of y = f(x) crosses the x-axis.
The first input to the iterative formula, written x0 or x1.
For the values of an iteration to get closer and closer to a single number as n increases.
For the values of an iteration to move away from any single value, so no root is found.
When f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs (one positive, one negative), showing the graph crosses the x-axis between a and b if f is continuous.
A function whose graph has no breaks or jumps, so it can be drawn without lifting the pen.
The set of numbers between two end values, e.g. between 0 and 1.
A numerical method that narrows the interval containing a root, one decimal place at a time, using the sign of f(x).
Testing values, comparing the result with the target and improving the estimate each time.
The calculator key that stores the last answer so that a formula can be repeated without retyping.
A rule giving the next term of a sequence from the previous term; an iterative formula is one.
A value that is close to, but not exactly, the true answer.
Ways of rounding a number to a stated accuracy.

worked.q: (a) Show that the equation x^3 + 5x - 3 = 0 has a solution between x = 0 and x = 1. (b) Show that the equation can be rearranged to x = (3 - x^3) / 5. (c) Using x(n+1) = (3 - x(n)^3) / 5 with x0 = 0, work out x1, x2 and x3. (d) Hence write down a solution to 2 decimal places. (7 marks)
steps: (a) Let f(x) = x^3 + 5x - 3. f(0) = 0 + 0 - 3 = -3 and f(1) = 1 + 5 - 3 = 3 (M1 for both values).
There is a change of sign and f is continuous, so a root lies between 0 and 1 (A1).
(d) Later values 0.5638, 0.5641, 0.5641 settle at 0.56 to 2 decimal places (B1).

worked.ans: f(0.555) = -0.054 and f(0.565) = 0.005: change of sign, so the root is 0.56 to 2 d.p.
worked.q: Show that the root of x^3 + 5x - 3 = 0 is 0.56 correct to 2 decimal places. (2 marks)
steps: The root rounds to 0.56 if it lies between 0.555 and 0.565.
There is a change of sign, f is continuous, so the root is between 0.555 and 0.565, hence 0.56 to 2 d.p. (A1).

worked.q: (a) Show that x^2 - 3x - 1 = 0 can be rearranged to x = 3 + 1/x. (b) Starting with x0 = 3 use x(n+1) = 3 + 1 / x(n) to find x1, x2 and x3. (c) Write the positive root correct to 2 decimal places. (6 marks)
steps: Divide every term by x: x = 3 + 1/x (A1).
(c) Next values 3.30275, 3.30278: the values agree to 3.30 (B1). Check: f(3.295) = -0.028, f(3.305) = 0.008, change of sign, so the root rounds to 3.30.
